title: Comments That Count: Giving Formative Feedback that Supports Revision and Learning
description: Dr. Matt McKinney, director of TAMU's Writing in the Disciplines program and an associate professor in the Department of English, will offer advice on providing students effective feedback. He'll discuss tools such as assignment scaffolding, peer workshops, progress reports, and student conferences, and consider how giving feedback has changed in the age of GenAI. Participants will have a chance to discuss their own insights and practice giving feedback on sample student texts. Lunch will be provided. Questions? Contact the UWC at uwc@tamu.edu or call 979-458-1455.

title: Lunch-and-Learn: Exploring the Potential of Gemini Notebook for Teaching and Learning
description: Discover how Gemini Notebook (formerly known as NotebookLM) can help you get more from the course materials you already have. In this interactive session, you will explore how Gemini Notebook can locate and summarize content, compare sources, generate teaching ideas, create lesson outlines, and answer questions grounded in your own documents. We will discuss best practices for using AI-generated content thoughtfully, including accessibility considerations. The workshop also includes examples of how students are using Gemini Notebook to support their learning and what that may mean for your teaching. This Lunch-and-Learn session includes a complimentary lunch provided by the Center for Teaching Excellence. Learning Outcomes: Participants will be able to… 1) Use Gemini Notebook to locate, summarize, and compare information from course materials. 2) Generate teaching resources, such as lesson outlines and instructional ideas, using Gemini Notebook. 3) Describe considerations for using Gemini Notebook responsibly in teaching and learning, including accessibility.

title: Dinner with a Prof
description: Ever wondered what your professors are like outside of the classroom? "Dinner with a Prof" is your chance to sit down with a faculty member over a relaxed meal, hear their personal story, and learn about what they’re passionate about. Each month, a different professor will share their experiences, offer advice, and talk about topics they care deeply about. It's a great opportunity to ask questions, get to know your professors as real people, and build connections that could last long after graduation. We’ve got you covered—dinner is on us, and we’ll take care of all the details, including any dietary restrictions. You just show up and enjoy the conversation! title: CIRTL National Presents: Teaching with Objects – An Eﬀective Teaching Method for Future Faculty
description: This interactive workshop is designed to equip graduate students and future faculty with the foundational skills and confidence to integrate object-based learning into their teaching across all disciplines. Moving beyond the misconception that object-based pedagogy is confined to art history or requires special expertise, this session introduces participants to the "See/Think/Wonder" framework—a versatile tool for facilitating evidence-based, student-centered discussion that can be applied in STEM, humanities, social sciences, and beyond. Participants will learn to design effective assignments, practice leading object-based discussions, and navigate campus resources and expert collaborations. The workshop emphasizes that effective teaching with objects relies not on the instructor's pre-existing content knowledge, but on their skill as a facilitator of observation and critical inquiry—a transferable skill applicable to any classroom setting. Optional pre-reading materials and a simple framework guide will be provided in advance to ensure all participants can engage meaningfully, regardless of prior experience. This session is ideal for anyone looking to create more engaged, interdisciplinary, and experiential learning environments in their future classrooms. By the end of this workshop, participants will be prepared to: Articulate the core philosophy of object-based learning as a student-centered, evidence-based pedagogical approach applicable beyond the arts and humanities Apply the "See/Think/Wonder" thinking routine to structure an object-based learning activity that fosters observation, interpretation, and questioning Design a scaffolded discussion prompt that uses an object to advance a specific learning goal in their discipline

title: Tech-Free Instructional Strategies for Engagement in the Classroom
description: Technology can be a tool used for engagement, but what happens when the Wi-Fi fails, a classroom tool is not available, or you simply need a different way to engage students? In collaboration with Elizabeth Garza and Dr. Laura Hammons, this workshop presents practical strategies to help faculty with student engagement regardless of available technology. Participants will explore a variety of low-stakes, low-preparation, and technology-free techniques that can serve as reliable alternatives or complements to digital tools. Together, we will discuss how these strategies can be adapted for a range of teaching environments, including large-enrollment courses, laboratory settings, and other instructional contexts. Learning Outcomes: Participants will be able to… 1) Identify a variety of low-stakes, technology-free instructional strategies that promote student engagement across different classroom settings. 2) Evaluate how the presented instructional strategies can be adapted to different instructional contexts. 3) Develop a plan that incorporates at least one technology-free engagement strategy into an upcoming class session.

title: American English Vowel System (Part 1 of 4)
description: The vowel sounds of American English are challenging to learners of English because there are so many, and because English spelling does not convey the pronunciation predictably. This four-session series of interactive workshops aims to increase attendees' phonological awareness, and as a result, their listening and intelligibility. Through a variety of activities and handouts, attendees will become familiar with each vowel and with resources to practice listening discrimination and pronunciation on their own. Each attendee has the opportunity to get personalized feedback on their own pronunciation. Those who attend Part 1 will automatically be registered for Parts 2-4 at the same time and place the following weeks.

title: Workshop: Doomscrolling, the Algorithm, and You
description: Many of us consume our news through our social media feeds. How do you know where that information originated? How is the algorithm influencing what you're seeing? Is it a conspiracy theory, AI generated, influencer click bait, or is it accurate news? We’re going to learn why it’s important to trace your sources, analyze how the algorithm is influencing our individual feeds, and practice how to look for the origins of what you’re seeing while social media doomscrolling.

title: Workshop: Leading with Integrity: Giving and Receiving Criticism
description: It’s hard to receive criticism without feeling defensive, ashamed, or angry, and it’s hard to give criticism without worrying about damaging your relationships. As a result, we don’t give criticism even when we know that we should, and we don’t learn from criticism that could have helped us grow. For groups, organizations, and leaders who value honesty and accountability, this is a serious problem, but there are steps that we can take to both give and receive criticism with greater ease and effectiveness.

title: Employee Engagement Staff Insights Virtual Workshop
description: The 2026 Employee Engagement Survey, conducted by organizational consulting firm Korn Ferry, provided valuable insights into the Texas A&M University employee experience that require deeper research and understanding. One of Korn Ferry’s findings that merits further exploration is the level of burnout reported by staff who frequently interact with a large number of students. To better understand these experiences, we are seeking staff volunteers to participate in survey insights workshops. Through these workshops, we hope to better understand the challenges staff face engaging with large numbers of students in their role and how these experiences shape their overall work environment. Insights gained from these discussions will help identify opportunities for the university to support staff well-being. Feedback gathered during these conversations will be aggregated and anonymized before being shared with the University Employee Experience Work Team. The information gathered will help shape recommendations and priorities for meaningful actions that support staff well-being, while enhancing the overall student experience.

title: GSPDT: Finding Your Teaching Voice: Understanding Strategies to Identify Your Pedagogical Approach
description: Teaching is not just about delivering content—it’s about connecting authentically with your students. Through guided reflection, short activities, and examples of pedagogical strategies, participants will explore how their knowledge, experiences, and disciplinary perspectives shape the way they teach. The session will also introduce techniques to manage expectations, establish an effective classroom tone, and select teaching approaches that align with their personality and goals as educators. Identify pedagogical strategies that align with their authentic style and disciplinary context. 3. Apply techniques to build confidence and classroom presence, including planning, body language, and interaction strategies.

title: Digital Accessibility Bytes: Checking for Content Accessibility in Canvas
description: Canvas provides built-in tools that can help instructors identify and resolve accessibility issues in the course. In this 30-minute session, participants will explore the accessibility tools available within Canvas and learn how to incorporate them into their course design workflow. We will examine the Canvas built-in accessibility checker, interpret Ally Course Accessibility Reports to identify common accessibility barriers, and apply recommendations to improve digital course content. Participants will also receive an introduction to YuJa Panorama and explore how it can support the remediation of course materials. Learning Outcomes: Participants will be able to… 1) Identify how to navigate and utilize Canvas’s built-in accessibility checker effectively. 2) Analyze and interpret accessibility reports generated by Ally.

title: The Higher-Impact Classroom: Elevating Current Practices Without Increasing Workload
description: Every instructor wants their students to deeply engage, retain knowledge, and succeed, yet the term "High-Impact Practices" can feel like an overwhelming mandate that requires a major remodeling of your course. This workshop strips away the administrative jargon to focus on a sustainable approach: making your existing courses higher-impact. By auditing the assignments and activities you already use, we will explore how small, intentional design tweaks can boost student engagement, success, and retention. Whether you teach a large lecture or a small seminar, this session offers a universal framework to elevate your teaching practices without inflating your grading workload. This foundational overview aligns with institutional goals while connecting you directly to customized CTE consultation support. Learning Outcomes: Participants will be able to… 1) Modify one existing course assignment to increase student engagement without increasing their grading workload.

title: Personalizing Learning with Adaptive Pathways in Canvas
description: Adaptive learning pathways provide a flexible way to personalize learning by guiding students to targeted resources and activities based on their performance, allowing each learner to receive the support or challenge they need while working toward the same learning outcomes. In this workshop, participants will explore how Canvas Mastery Paths can be used to design adaptive learning experiences that respond to student learning in real time. Dr. Darren Henrichs will showcase how a low-stakes assessment, or check-for-understanding, can trigger personalized learning pathways that incorporate multimedia resources, practice opportunities, and extension activities. Participants will examine the instructional decisions behind an adaptive learning module; they will then design an adaptive learning pathway. Learning Outcomes: Participants will be able to… 1) Explain the principles of adaptive learning pathways. 2) Discuss potential uses of adaptive learning pathways. 3) Design an adaptive learning pathway using a low-stakes assessment to direct students to the right resources.
classification_reasoning_summary: Event is academic, research, or career oriented.

title: American English Vowel System (Part 2 of 4)
description: The vowel sounds of American English are challenging to learners of English because there are so many, and because English spelling does not convey the pronunciation predictably. This four-session series of interactive workshops aims to increase attendees' phonological awareness, and as a result, their listening and intelligibility. Through a variety of activities and handouts, attendees will become familiar with each vowel and with resources to practice listening discrimination and pronunciation on their own. Each attendee has the opportunity to get personalized feedback on their own pronunciation. This event is restricted to those who attended Part 1 (register for that at https://ers.tamu.edu/event/10678).
classification_reasoning_summary: Event is academic, research, or career oriented.

title: Workshop: Leading with Integrity: Giving and Receiving Criticism
description: It’s hard to receive criticism without feeling defensive, ashamed, or angry, and it’s hard to give criticism without worrying about damaging your relationships. As a result, we don’t give criticism even when we know that we should, and we don’t learn from criticism that could have helped us grow. For groups, organizations, and leaders who value honesty and accountability, this is a serious problem, but there are steps that we can take to both give and receive criticism with greater ease and effectiveness.
classification_reasoning_summary: Event is academic, research, or career oriented.

title: Stop Refereeing Group Projects: A Plug-and-Play Toolkit for Student Self-Managing Teams
description: This workshop explores how to design and facilitate small group projects that empower students to manage their own team dynamics, workflows, and internal conflicts. Moving beyond generic project guidelines, participants will examine evidence-based strategies to help student teams self-diagnose and self-correct using vetted, classroom-ready working style inventories and peer charters. We will address common pain points—such as free-riders, communication breakdowns, and grading friction—by introducing modular, just-in-time tools that can be deployed immediately to course-correct current groups or archived to launch seamless collaboration next semester. Faculty will walk away with access to a pre-organized digital toolkit containing plug-and-play communication templates, workflow matrices, and student-led escalation protocols designed to shift the instructor's role from group referee to strategic consultant. Learning Outcomes: Participants will be able to… 1) Design student peer charters and escalation/deescalation protocols to reduce instructor conflict management.
classification_reasoning_summary: Event is academic, research, or career oriented.

title: NACADA Webinar: The Art of Saying No: Navigating Difficult Academic Advising Conversations
description: Difficult conversations are an inevitable part of academic advising, but they often come with a heavy emotional toll. Whether delivering disappointing news about academic policies, discussing a student's poor performance, or addressing issues like academic dismissal, these challenging interactions can lead to burnout and emotional exhaustion. In this webinar, we aim to equip academic advisors with practical tools and strategies to navigate these tough conversations while managing their emotional well-being. Utilizing Compassionate Directness, the SPIKES protocol, and BRIGHT advising approach, we address the art of saying "no." At the end the webinar, we aim for participants to have actionable insights, self-reflection tools, and self-care strategies designed to enhance their ability to handle challenging conversations and create a healthier, more effective advising environment. Participants will be able to: - Identify personal strengths and areas for improvement in handling difficult conversations, based on self-assessment of common advising scenarios. - Demonstrate the ability to apply at least three effective communication strategies for difficult conversations, including techniques for saying no assertively, through worksheet and role-play exercises. - Create a self-care plan that includes strategies to maintain well-being when engaging in difficult conversations and creating a supportive advising environment.
classification_reasoning_summary: Event centers on wellness or fitness.

title: Employee Engagement Staff Insights Virtual Workshop
description: The 2026 Employee Engagement Survey, conducted by organizational consulting firm Korn Ferry, provided valuable insights into the Texas A&M University employee experience that require deeper research and understanding. One of Korn Ferry’s findings that merits further exploration is the level of burnout reported by staff who frequently interact with a large number of students. To better understand these experiences, we are seeking staff volunteers to participate in survey insights workshops. Through these workshops, we hope to better understand the challenges staff face engaging with large numbers of students in their role and how these experiences shape their overall work environment. Insights gained from these discussions will help identify opportunities for the university to support staff well-being. Feedback gathered during these conversations will be aggregated and anonymized before being shared with the University Employee Experience Work Team. The information gathered will help shape recommendations and priorities for meaningful actions that support staff well-being, while enhancing the overall student experience.

description: True workforce readiness requires more than technical competency—modern employers are actively seeking graduates who can navigate ambiguity, collaborate across differences, and solve complex community challenges. title: Workshop: Leading with Integrity: Giving and Receiving Criticism
description: It’s hard to receive criticism without feeling defensive, ashamed, or angry, and it’s hard to give criticism without worrying about damaging your relationships. As a result, we don’t give criticism even when we know that we should, and we don’t learn from criticism that could have helped us grow. For groups, organizations, and leaders who value honesty and accountability, this is a serious problem, but there are steps that we can take to both give and receive criticism with greater ease and effectiveness.
classification_reasoning_summary: Event is academic, research, or career oriented.

title: Workshop: When Loyalties Collide: What Does It Mean to Lead in an Era of Conflicting Loyalties?
description: Our loyalties profoundly shape how we interpret events, information, and people, often in ways we don't recognize. Studies consistently show that two people with different loyalties can witness the same situation and reach completely opposite conclusions. This makes it essential for leaders to critically examine their own loyalties: Why are we loyal to certain ideas, people, or groups? Are these loyalties justified? When should we reconsider or even abandon a loyalty? In this workshop we will explore various definitions and theories of loyalty, which will help you to develop practical frameworks for navigating conflicting loyalties and leading with moral clarity.
classification_reasoning_summary: Event is academic, research, or career oriented.

description: Do you have questions about English grammar that haven't been covered in a workshop or need additional practice with a challenging grammar topic? Special Topics in Grammar for Speech is an interactive drop-in session where participants can ask questions about grammar for spoken communication and receive individualized guidance. Discussions may focus on topics such as verb tenses, modal verbs, question formation, articles, passive voice, or any other grammar questions participants bring. Monitor and revise their own spoken grammar while communicating in academic and professional contexts.

title: GSPDT: Creating Accessible PDFs and Canvas Courses
description: The recent Title II revision (the Final Rule) mandates that all digital content meet accessibility standards, ensuring usability for all learners. This workshop focuses on two key areas of digital accessibility: PDF documents and Canvas course design. PDF files are often the most challenging materials to remediate, and participants will explore common accessibility issues found in PDFs while practicing with Adobe Acrobat’s built-in accessibility checker. The session will also introduce accessibility tools in Canvas, including the platform’s accessibility checker and the Ally report. Participants will learn how to interpret accessibility feedback, apply recommended fixes, and improve the overall accessibility of their course content. Learning Outcomes: Participants will be able to… 1) Identify common accessibility issues found in PDF documents and explain why they create barriers for learners. 2) Use Adobe Acrobat’s accessibility checker to evaluate and remediate PDF files. 3) Apply accessibility best practices within Canvas, including the use of the platform’s accessibility checker. 4) Interpret Ally reports and implement recommended improvements to enhance the accessibility of course materials.
classification_reasoning_summary: Event is academic, research, or career oriented.

title: TREC Seminar - Alfredo Erazo-Oliveras, PhD & Hasara Abeygunaratne
description: The Texas A&M Regional Center of Excellence in Cancer invites you to enjoy a unique style of TREC Seminar. Hosted in Rudder Tower, Room #701, on Thursday, November 12, TREC will highlight our two Judge's Choice award winners from the 4th Annual TREC "Advances in Cancer Research" Symposium poster session back in April. Hasara Abeygunaratne (Texas A&M Dept. Cell Biology & Genetics) is a fourth-year Ph.D. Candidate in Medical Sciences at the Naresh K. Vashisht College of Medicine, Texas A&M University. Her doctoral research investigates how microglial NF-κB-inducing kinase (NIK) regulates glioblastoma progression. At this seminar, we look forward to hearing about her work on "Microglial NF-κB-Inducing Kinase (NIK) Promotes Male-Biased Glioblastoma Tumor Pathogenesis". Dr. Alfredo Erazo-Oliveras (Texas A&M Dept. Nutrition) is an Associate Research Scientist in the Program in Integrative Nutrition & Complex Diseases. His current research focuses on investigating the effects of key driver oncogenes and membrane active dietaries (MADs) on stem cell signaling/homeostasis and colorectal carcinogenesis. At this seminar, we look forward to hearing about his work on "A Greasy "Tug of War": Plasma Membrane-Centric Novel Mechanisms Describing The Effects Of Diet On The Wnt Signaling Pathway, Stemness and Carcinogenesis". Registration is not required for this seminar. Remote attendance can be accessed via the following Zoom link: https://tamu.zoom.us/j/96464257891 To add this event to your calendar, please complete this short form: tx.ag/TREClearners

description: In this online panel, we'll hear from CIRTL alumni who hold STEM PhDs and work in centers for teaching and learning at research universities. Centers for teaching and learning are an increasingly common office in universities – providing evidence-based support and guidance to faculty and others with instructional responsibilities – and are one of many ways people with PhDs work within higher ed, but beyond the professoriate. Alumni will share what their jobs are like, how they became interested in this unique type of work, how their doctoral training prepared them for their roles, and what growth and progression can look like in these types of career paths. This is the third event in our four-part series "Exploring Career Paths with CIRTL Alumni."

title: Civic Conversation: What's Next, America?
description: Across the country, since before our nation was founded, Americans have been working together to solve problems they faced in their communities. From everyday citizens participating in New England town meetings to the speeches and sit-ins of the Civil Rights Movement, communities have proven they can stick together and work together – even in the most challenging of times. As our nation turns 250, many Americans believe that the time is right for conversations that bring people together who might not normally talk and work together, conversations that will encourage fresh, innovative thinking and actions to emerge. “What’s Next, America?” is designed to do just that — connect people who are already working to develop strong communities while bringing new people and new ideas into the mix.

title: American English Vowel System (Part 4 of 4)
description: The vowel sounds of American English are challenging to learners of English because there are so many, and because English spelling does not convey the pronunciation predictably. This four-session series of interactive workshops aims to increase attendees' phonological awareness, and as a result, their listening and intelligibility. Through a variety of activities and handouts, attendees will become familiar with each vowel and with resources to practice listening discrimination and pronunciation on their own. Each attendee has the opportunity to get personalized feedback on their own pronunciation. title: Workshop: Leading with Integrity: Giving and Receiving Criticism
description: It’s hard to receive criticism without feeling defensive, ashamed, or angry, and it’s hard to give criticism without worrying about damaging your relationships. As a result, we don’t give criticism even when we know that we should, and we don’t learn from criticism that could have helped us grow. For groups, organizations, and leaders who value honesty and accountability, this is a serious problem, but there are steps that we can take to both give and receive criticism with greater ease and effectiveness.

title: Workshop: When Loyalties Collide: What Does It Mean to Lead in an Era of Conflicting Loyalties?
description: Our loyalties profoundly shape how we interpret events, information, and people, often in ways we don't recognize. Studies consistently show that two people with different loyalties can witness the same situation and reach completely opposite conclusions. This makes it essential for leaders to critically examine their own loyalties: Why are we loyal to certain ideas, people, or groups? Are these loyalties justified? title: NACADA Webinar: From Chaos to Clarity: Building Scalable Advising Systems for Large Caseloads
description: Large advising caseloads are an increasing reality across higher education, often creating tension between operational demands and advisor well-being. As practitioner literature and national conversations continue to highlight the connection between high-volume caseloads and advisor burnout, institutions are seeking structured and sustainable solutions. This webinar explores how advising units can intentionally align operational efficiency with practices that protect advisor capacity while maintaining high-quality student support. Drawing on experiences within an advising center serving undergraduate business students at a large public institution, presenters will outline scalable strategies that promote clarity, consistency, and shared responsibility. Participants will examine structured appointment models, including required versus optional advising touchpoints, as well as tiered advising approaches such as individual, group, and walk-in formats. Presenters will also share cross-team support systems designed to address uneven caseload distribution. In addition, the session will explore advising delivery formats that support accessibility and efficiency, with examples drawn from our in-person and email advising models. The webinar will further highlight the role of standardized documentation practices, centralized resource hubs, and clearly defined advising boundaries in reducing redundancy and preventing burnout. Emphasis will be placed on practical frameworks that can be adapted to institutions of varying sizes and resources levels. Participants will leave with actionable strategies for designing advising systems that balance efficiency with advisor well-being in large caseload environments. Participants Will Be Able To: - Assess structural factors within their advising units that contribute to inefficiency or advisor burnout in large caseload environments. - Design structured appointment models that align required advising touchpoints with institutional capacity and student needs. - Apply tiered advising approaches (e.g., individual, group, and walk-in formats) to improve scalability and resource allocation. - Develop cross-team support systems and standardized documentation practices that promote clarity, shared responsibility, and consistency. - Establish sustainable boundaries and operational practices that protect advisor well-being while maintaining high-quality student support.
classification_reasoning_summary: Event is academic, research, or career oriented.

title: NACADA Webinar: Empowering the Mid-Level: Creating Sustainable Professional Pathways
description: Academic advising professionals are often celebrated for their commitment, longevity, and deep institutional knowledge. While some advisors aspire to senior leadership roles, others find fulfillment in remaining “helping professionals” focused on direct student support. When traditional promotional pathways are limited or unavailable, feelings of stagnation and diminished recognition can emerge. This webinar will reframe career advancement by exploring the value of horizontal and lateral career movement as intentional strategies for professional development through the lens of (a) advising administrators, (b) professional advisors, and (c) faculty advisors. Participants will engage in a reflective, practical career-success planning aimed at redefining growth beyond the conventional “climbing the ladder” model. Explore meaningful ways to build a rich, rewarding career that aligns with personal values, institutional needs, and long-term sustainability. Participants Will Be Able To: - Understand the complexity of being an advising middle manager. - Understand the intersection between advising models and institutional management structures. - Discuss the history and development of mid-career practitioners within academic advising and other niches of higher education. - Develop strategies to overcome professional challenges. - Gain insights on sustainable approaches to keep current and future advising practitioners within the field.
classification_reasoning_summary: Event is academic, research, or career oriented.

title: NACADA Webinar: Practical Strategies for Trauma-Informed Advising
description: As advisors, students frequently reveal the traumatic events of their lives to us. Without professional licensure in mental health services, what should advisors do? For students to access resources that will address their mental health needs, they first need to reveal to a trusted person that they need help. For this reason, it is incredibly important for advisors to know how to use trauma-informed practices to create a safe space for all students to ask for help. At the basis of trauma-informed advising is intentionally enacting the 5 principles of trauma-informed care in our advising practice, including safety, trustworthiness, choice, collaboration, and empowerment” “Harris & Fallot, 2001”. All of these principles are relational skills at their core, highlighting the importance of relational advising strategies when working with students who have experienced trauma. While the practice of trauma-informed advising is primarily relational, it is often difficult to know how to practically enact trauma-informed conversational strategies with students during high-stress advising moments. This session is ideal for advisors who desire to deepen their understanding of trauma and its impact on students, while learning powerful conversational techniques to better empathize with students in distress. Participants Will Be Able To: - Identify what trauma is, how it impacts our stress-response system, and signs of a student in distress. - Use conversational techniques such as validation, scaling questions, externalization, and parts language to empathize with students while also maintaining appropriate boundaries. - Enact practical strategies for taking a trauma-informed and person-centered approach in our work as advisors. - Make effective referrals to mental health services.
classification_reasoning_summary: Event is academic, research, or career oriented.

title: NACADA Webinar: Rethinking Student Centered: Building an Advisor-Centered Culture for Meaningful Stu
description: Higher education practitioners have historically promoted student-centered philosophies and practices. While well-intentioned, focusing solely on student needs does not account for the professionals who are both responsible for and invested in student learning. We intentionally shifted our focus to be advisor-centered: when advisors are respected and valued within a community of care, they will experience a sense of belonging and be deeply engaged in their profession. This culture mitigates burnout and enhances recruitment, resilience, and retention. Valuing advisor development and well-being benefits both the advising community and students. Cultural change requires ongoing systemic and structural transformation, self-reflection, compassion, and intentional leadership. This presentation explores the benefits of an advisor-centered approach and offers strategies for embedding it into practice. Participants will gain actionable insights to create a sustainable, engaged, and impactful advising community within their organizations. Participants Will Be Able To: - Appreciate the importance of a work culture. - Learn why a culture of support is critical. - Understand the many ways in which culture can be fostered, and that it is difficult, takes time, and is ultimately extraordinarily rewarding. - Reflect upon the kind of a work culture participants might want to foster in their own work environments, given the personalities of the leadership and staff.
classification_reasoning_summary: Event is academic, research, or career oriented.

title: NACADA Webinar: Advising Undecided Reimagined: Framework, Praxis, and Storytelling for Exploring Stu
description: In 2023 the First Year Advising Center and Career and Life Design at Oakland University were tasked with coming up with a strategy to better support and retain our Undecided (Exploring) student population. Our division leadership created an initiative to develop better lines of communication between departments and to model effective collaboration in a common goal of retaining and supporting this unique student population. Early on our goal was to define the overarching reason we did not retain our Exploring student population at the same rate as their peers. In the years following the initial pilot program we developed resources, strengthened campus partnerships, and best practices for academic advisers and career coaches. These resources have evolved over time and we are excited to share what has proven to be most effective. This session will provide a brief overview of how we built the foundation of our program along with highlighting strategies our colleagues across campus can use to help guide students in the decision making process for major selection. You will learn and practice three unique techniques designed to better support and engage Exploring and Redeciding students. Participants Will Be Able To: - Learn how one advising office leveraged campus partnerships to create and maintain institutional buy-in for a new initiative. - Understand how collaboration with the Career and Life Design Center led to a stronger referral process, increased communication and outreach for students, and more congruent one-stop services. - Use research to create advising tools, resources, and new techniques that helped build new adviser training models. - Understand how Advisors approached building new appointment structures and the content in each student appointment. - Understand how to track student progress data and use it effectively. - Understand why changing the culture and stigma of being Undecided (Exploring) matters for this generation of college students. - Practice advising resources, and techniques that have been successful over the past three years via storytelling, dreaming and brainstorming.
classification_reasoning_summary: Event is academic, research, or career oriented.
